qs.q: Where is the niche for Epstein-Barr virus in humans?
qs.e: EBV establishes latency in B lymphocytes (lymphoid tissue) and reactivates in salivary gland epithelium, explaining why it is shed in saliva and transmitted via kissing. This dual tropism is central to its biology.

es.q: Discuss Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma, detailing its key epidemiological association, the role of Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) in its pathogenesis, and the distinguishing histological features of its most common variant. Conclude with a brief overview of its clinical behavior and prognosis.
es.m: Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (NPC) exhibits a strong epidemiological association with high incidence in Chinese populations, linking it to viral oncogenesis and genetic susceptibility. The role of Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) in its pathogenesis is critical. EBV genome is found in virtually all cases of NPC. The virus first replicates in the nasopharyngeal epithelium and then infects tonsillar B lymphocytes, leading to epithelial transformation and the development of carcinoma. NPC has three histological variants: keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma, non-keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma, and undifferentiated carcinoma. ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Epstein‑Barr virus (EBV) is a ubiquitous herpesvirus that infects B‑cells, causing infectious mononucleosis and driving malignancies like endemic Burkitt lymphoma. Understanding its transmission, diagnosis, and management is essential, especially in low‑resource settings where co‑factors such as malaria increase risk.

sections.p: EBV is a DNA virus of the Herpesviridae family that establishes lifelong latency in B‑lymphocytes. Primary infection is usually asymptomatic in childhood, but in adolescents it can cause infectious mononucleosis.
b: Transmitted via saliva, blood, organ transplant

sections.p: A double‑stranded DNA virus with an envelope bearing glycoproteins that bind CD21 on B‑cells. It can drive uncontrolled B‑cell proliferation through c‑myc translocation.
b: Infects B‑cells, epithelial cells, NK cells

sections.p: Spread occurs mainly through saliva (kissing, sharing utensils) and less commonly via blood or organ transplantation. After acute replication, the virus enters latency in memory B‑cells.
b: Latency phases I–III with different viral gene expression

sections.p: EBV causes infectious mononucleosis, contributes to endemic Burkitt lymphoma (especially with chronic malaria), nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and can trigger hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.
b: Acute: fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly
Chronic: B‑cell lymphomas, especially in malaria‑endemic regions

sections.p: Combine clinical picture with serology and, when needed, tissue biopsy. In low‑resource settings, rely on simple blood counts and heterophile antibody test.

t.b: Does the patient have acute EBV infection? Positive test supports mononucleosis; false‑negative early in disease.

t.a: EBV VCA IgM/IgG, EBNA IgG serology
t.b: What stage of infection? IgM positive = acute; IgG alone = past infection; EBNA IgG appears >6 weeks.
Is there atypical lymphocytosis? Presence of reactive CD8+ T cells supports infectious mononucleosis.
Is there EBV‑driven lymphoma? Positive EBER confirms EBV involvement in Burkitt lymphoma.

sections.p: Supportive care is mainstay for mononucleosis; antiviral therapy is reserved for severe or immunocompromised cases. Lymphoma requires chemotherapy, with attention to malaria co‑infection in endemic areas.
b: Hydration, analgesia, avoid contact sports for splenic protection
Consider rituximab (anti‑CD20) for EBV‑positive lymphoproliferative disease
In low‑resource settings, treat malaria aggressively to reduce lymphoma risk

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and clinical practice.
b: Positive heterophile test + atypical lymphocytes = infectious mononucleosis.
Endemic Burkitt lymphoma: translocation t(8;14) c‑myc + EBV + chronic malaria.
Avoid steroids in acute mononucleosis unless airway compromise.

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent high fever >38.5°C with lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly
Neurological signs (confusion, seizures) suggesting CNS involvement

faq.a: No vaccine exists; reduce saliva sharing and practice safe transfusion practices.

faq.q: Why is Burkitt lymphoma more common where malaria is endemic?
faq.a: Chronic malaria suppresses immune control of EBV‑infected B‑cells, increasing malignant transformation.

faq.q: Is a negative Monospot test definitive?
faq.a: No; early infection may be negative. Confirm with EBV‑specific serology.

exam: Explain how EBV contributes to the pathogenesis of endemic Burkitt lymphoma.
List the diagnostic criteria for infectious mononucleosis and how they differ from CMV mononucleosis.
Describe the management steps for a patient with suspected splenic rupture due to EBV.
